script.opening: "Doctor, these headaches are destroying me. It’s an unbelievable pain behind my right eye — like a hot poker — comes on most nights around 2am, lasts an hour or so, my eye goes red and streams, my nose runs on that side. I literally pace the room and bang my head on the wall, I can’t sit still. Painkillers do nothing. They’ve been coming for two weeks straight."

facts.text: Two weeks. Always the RIGHT eye and temple. Builds to its worst within minutes, lasts 45 minutes to an hour and a half, then goes completely. Usually around 2am, sometimes a second one mid-afternoon. "Ten out of ten — worse than when I broke my leg."

Right eye red and watering, eyelid droops, right nostril runs or blocks. Can’t lie still — paces, rocks, presses on the eye, has banged his head on the wall. No nausea, no vomiting, light doesn’t bother him particularly.
If asked: "Something like this happened about 2 years ago for a few weeks in spring — I thought it was my sinuses and it went away." No headaches between bouts.

Never a sudden thunderclap headache. No weakness, numbness, speech or vision loss between attacks. No fever, no rash, no neck stiffness. No head injury. Between attacks he feels normal, "just shattered".
Tried paracetamol, ibuprofen and some co-codamol his wife had — "nothing touches it". No regular medicines. No heart problems, no chest pain, no high blood pressure known. No asthma. No allergies.

Smokes 20 a day. Drinks 3–4 pints on Friday and Saturday — noticed a beer brought on an attack within an hour last week. Coffee 4 cups a day. Works as a delivery van driver — exhausted and worried about falling asleep at the wheel. Lives with his wife, Aneta, and their baby, in a flat (has a gas cooker).
"Some nights I’ve thought I can’t take much more." No plan, would not act on it, "I just want it to stop." Has not harmed himself.

Exhausted, desperate, a bit tearful but trying to hold it together. You think it may be migraine or sinuses, and at 3am you think it’s a tumour. When oxygen is mentioned, ask: "I smoke — is that a problem?" Feel huge relief if the doctor names the condition and explains why ordinary painkillers haven’t worked.

ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — "At 3am I start thinking it’s a brain tumour." He is at the end of his tether and frightened by his own thoughts; worried about losing his driving job.

cues: "I bang my head on the wall" — restlessness typical of cluster headache, and how desperate he is.
"Some nights I’ve thought I can’t take much more" (if mood is explored) — needs a direct question about suicidal thoughts.
"I smoke — is that a problem?" (when oxygen is discussed) — fire safety with home oxygen.

checkpoints.text: Recognises CLUSTER HEADACHE — strictly unilateral, excruciating orbital/temporal pain, short-lived (15–180 min), circadian/nocturnal, with ipsilateral cranial autonomic features and RESTLESSNESS/agitation, in clusters

DISTINGUISHES it from migraine (longer, throbbing, lies still in a dark room, nausea/photophobia) and from sinusitis — using the autonomic features and restlessness with short severe attacks as discriminators

Knows the ACUTE treatment differs (NICE CG150) — 100% OXYGEN at 12 L/min or more via a non-rebreathing mask with reservoir bag and/or a fast-acting (SUBCUTANEOUS/NASAL) TRIPTAN abort attacks — and that paracetamol, NSAIDs, opioids, ergots and oral triptans should not be offered; addresses the home-oxygen fire risk in a smoker

Considers PREVENTIVE treatment during a bout (VERAPAMIL, NICE CG150, with specialist advice first if unfamiliar and ECG monitoring; steroid course/GON block to break a cluster, specialist) and starts prevention early

Advises on triggers (alcohol during a bout, smoking), SCREENS headache red flags warranting imaging, discusses neuroimaging for a first bout with a headache GPwSI or neurologist (NICE CG150), and refers to NEUROLOGY for confirmation/management
Responds to extreme distress with empathy, SCREENS mood/suicidality given the severity ("suicide headache"), and conveys that effective treatment exists
Explains why this is not migraine/sinusitis and why the treatment is different, checking understanding

Safety-nets and follows up: arranges home oxygen + suitable triptan, neurology referral, prevention with monitoring, red-flag and mood/crisis safety-netting, and review — correct O2/triptan plan, not another opioid script

worked.txt: "What you’re describing isn’t an ordinary headache or migraine — the strictly one-sided pain behind the eye, the red watering eye and runny nostril, the short attacks at the same time each night, and pacing because you can’t keep still — that’s cluster headache. It’s one of the most severe pains there is, and crucially it needs specific treatment."
"That’s why your painkillers do nothing — the attacks are too short and intense for tablets to work, and opioids actually aren’t the answer. We use two things that genuinely abort an attack."

"First, high-flow oxygen through a special mask at the start of an attack — I’ll arrange that for home and for when you’re out. Because you smoke, I need to be honest: smoking or any flame near oxygen is a real fire risk, so it can’t happen in the same room. Second, a fast triptan, given as an injection under the skin or a nasal spray, not a tablet. Together these can switch attacks off."

"To stop them coming during this run, we can consider a preventer — verapamil — and I’ll get the specialist’s advice on it first, with heart tracings as we increase it. Starting it early in a bout helps. Avoid alcohol while you’re in a cluster, as it triggers attacks, and smoking doesn’t help."

"This level of pain is genuinely tormenting — it’s sometimes called the ‘suicide headache’. Can I ask honestly, has it ever made you feel life isn’t worth living? … Thank you. I want to support you, not just the headaches."

"I’ll refer you to neurology to confirm and manage this, and discuss with them whether you need a scan as it’s your first bout. I’d also like to examine you in person. If you ever get a sudden ‘worst-ever’ thunderclap headache, new weakness, or it changes character, that’s different — seek urgent help. And if your mood drops or you feel unsafe, contact us straight away."

f.learning: CLUSTER HEADACHE — a trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia — presents with STRICTLY UNILATERAL, EXCRUCIATING orbital/temporal pain, SHORT-LIVED (typically 15–180 min, often ~45–90), occurring once to several times daily with CIRCADIAN/nocturnal timing, accompanied by ipsilateral CRANIAL AUTONOMIC features (red/watering eye, ptosis/lid swelling, nasal congestion/rhinorrhoea, miosis) and marked RESTLESSNESS/agitation, occurring in CLUSTERS over weeks; it is commoner in men and smokers. The key contrast is with MIGRAINE, which is usually LONGER (4–72 h), throbbing, with nausea/photophobia, and where the patient prefers to LIE STILL in a dark room — whereas cluster attacks are short, strictly one-sided with autonomic features, and the patient is AGITATED — so do not mislabel it as migraine or sinusitis. Critically, the ACUTE treatment is DIFFERENT and high-yield (NICE CG150, 2012, updated June 2025): 100% OXYGEN at a flow rate of at least 12 litres per minute through a non-rebreathing mask with a reservoir bag and/or a fast-acting SUBCUTANEOUS or NASAL TRIPTAN (sumatriptan) abort attacks, while paracetamol, NSAIDs, opioids, ergots and oral triptans should not be offered; home oxygen in a smoker carries a serious fire risk. Consider PREVENTIVE treatment during a bout — VERAPAMIL (NICE CG150: seek specialist advice first if unfamiliar with it, including ECG monitoring for heart block), with a steroid course or greater occipital nerve block to break a cluster — started early. Advise on triggers (alcohol during a bout, smoking), screen headache red flags warranting imaging (thunderclap/first-and-worst, focal neurology, new in older age, abnormal exam, raised-ICP/GCA features), discuss neuroimaging for a first bout with a headache GPwSI or neurologist (NICE CG150), and refer to neurology. Given the extreme severity (the "suicide headache"), screen mood and suicidality (NICE NG225) and support the patient — not another opioid prescription.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE CG150 (headaches in over 12s: diagnosis and management, 2012, updated June 2025) · [2] NICE NG225 (self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence, 2022) · [3] International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (International Headache Society, 2018) (international)
knowledge.summary: Strictly one-sided, severe pain around the eye lasting about an hour, at the same time each night for two weeks, with a red watering eye, a runny nostril on the same side and pacing restlessness, is cluster headache. Name it, explain why tablets fail, and give the acute plan NICE CG150 sets out: high-flow oxygen and/or a subcutaneous or nasal triptan. Consider verapamil for prevention with specialist advice and ECG monitoring, screen red flags and mood, and deal with the smoking and home-oxygen safety issue.

points.t: Attacks of severe unilateral orbital, supraorbital or temporal pain lasting roughly 15–180 minutes, from every other day up to several a day, with ipsilateral autonomic features (tearing, red eye, nasal blockage or discharge, lid swelling or drooping, small pupil) and/or restlessness or agitation [3]. Bouts often last weeks and recur at the same time of day. It is commoner in men and in smokers.

Migraine usually lasts hours to days, is often throbbing with nausea and light sensitivity, and the person lies still in a dark room. In cluster headache the person cannot keep still, the attacks are short and strictly one-sided, and the autonomic signs are on the painful side. Sinusitis does not wake someone at the same hour every night with a streaming eye.

NICE CG150 [1]: offer oxygen and/or a subcutaneous or nasal triptan. Oxygen is 100% at a flow rate of at least 12 litres per minute through a non-rebreathing mask with a reservoir bag, with home and ambulatory oxygen arranged. Make sure the triptan supply is enough for the attack frequency. Do not offer paracetamol, NSAIDs, opioids, ergots or oral triptans for acute attacks [1]. Check triptan cautions such as ischaemic heart disease and uncontrolled hypertension (BNF).

NICE CG150 [1]: consider verapamil for prevention during a bout; if unfamiliar with its use for cluster headache, seek specialist advice first, including advice on ECG monitoring, because heart block can develop as the dose rises (BNF). Seek specialist advice if verapamil does not work. Steroid courses and occipital nerve blocks are specialist options to break a bout.

NICE CG150 [1]: discuss the need for neuroimaging for a first bout of cluster headache with a GP with a special interest in headache or a neurologist. Red flags needing urgent assessment include thunderclap onset, new neurological deficit, fever with neck stiffness, a changing pattern, features of raised pressure, and new headache in older age.

Home oxygen is ordered through the home oxygen order process with a safety risk assessment. Smoking, vaping or naked flames near oxygen are a serious fire risk, so an honest conversation about smoking is a safety step as well as a health one.

The pain is among the most severe known and hopelessness during a bout is common. Ask directly about suicidal thoughts; NICE NG225 [2] advises against using risk scales to predict outcome — assess needs and agree a safety plan.
Alcohol commonly triggers attacks during a bout but not between bouts, so advise avoiding it while a bout is active. Support to stop smoking.

Asked about sleep, work, smoking and alcohol, and how the bout was affecting daily life.
Examined pupils, lids, fundi and neurology; checked BP before triptan; noted ECG monitoring for verapamil.
Cluster headache versus migraine, sinusitis, trigeminal neuralgia and secondary headache.
Screened thunderclap onset, focal neurology, visual change, fever and neck stiffness; screened suicidality.
Cluster headache (first bout) explained clearly, including why tablets fail.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Subcutaneous or nasal triptan and high-flow 100% oxygen at 12 L/min or more (NICE CG150); no opioids or oral analgesics; verapamil with specialist advice.
Smoking and oxygen fire risk with cessation support; alcohol during a bout; fit note; neuroimaging discussion for a first bout.

ro.d: Picked up ‘destroying me’, head-banging and 3am fears; asked directly about suicidal thoughts.
Idea: migraine or sinuses. Concern: a tumour and the unbearable pain. Expectation: for the pain to stop.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — "At 3am I start thinking it’s a brain tumour." He is at the end of his tether and frightened by his own thoughts; worried about losing his driving job — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mr Solomon, I’m Dr Patel. Please, take a seat. What’s been happening?
model.why: Open question; lets him tell the story

model.text: Doctor, these headaches are destroying me. It’s like a hot poker behind my right eye, most nights about 2am, for an hour or so. My eye goes red and streams, my nose runs on that side. I pace the room and bang my head on the wall. Painkillers do nothing. Two weeks of this.

That sounds unbearable, and you look exhausted. I think I already have an idea what this is, and there is treatment that works. Can I ask a few specific questions, then explain and agree a plan with you?
model.why: Acknowledges distress, offers hope and sets the agenda

model.text: Please. Anything.
Is it always the right side, never the left? And does it come on quickly and stop within a few hours?
model.why: Confirms strict laterality and short duration

model.text: Always the right. It builds in minutes, and it’s gone within about an hour, sometimes a bit longer.
During an attack, do you want to lie still in a dark room, or can you not keep still? Any sickness or problem with light?
model.why: Uses restlessness versus stillness to separate it from migraine

model.text: I can’t stay still. I walk up and down, rock, anything. I don’t feel sick.
Have you had runs of headaches like this before, maybe in a previous year?
Nothing like this that I can remember.
A few safety questions. Did any headache start suddenly like a thunderclap? Any weakness, numbness, double vision, loss of vision, fever or stiff neck? Any change in your vision between attacks?
model.why: Screens red flags for secondary headache

model.text: No. Between attacks I’m fine, just shattered.
What have you been thinking this might be?
Migraine, maybe, or my sinuses. And then at 3am I start thinking it’s a tumour.

That’s a very natural fear with pain this bad. Can I ask something I ask everyone with this kind of pain? When it’s at its worst, has it ever made you feel you can’t go on, or that life isn’t worth living?
model.why: Names the fear and asks directly about suicidal thoughts

model.text: (pause) Some nights I’ve thought I can’t take much more. I wouldn’t do anything. I just want it to stop.

Thank you for telling me honestly. That’s what this pain does to people, and it’s part of why I want to get proper treatment in place today. If those thoughts ever got stronger, I’d want you to ring us or NHS 111, or 999 if you felt unsafe. Is that okay?
model.why: Responds with empathy and agrees a safety plan

model.text: Yes. Okay.

I’d like to examine your eyes, face and nervous system. … Your pupils, eye movements and the back of your eyes look normal, and the nerve checks are normal. Together with your story, this fits cluster headache, not migraine and not a tumour or sinuses.
model.why: Examines and names the diagnosis with the reasoning

model.text: Cluster headache? I’ve never heard of it.

It’s a headache that comes in bouts — often weeks at a time — usually at the same time each day. The pain is one-sided around the eye, with the eye watering and the nose running on that side, and people can’t keep still. Tablets fail because each attack is too short and too fierce for a tablet to be absorbed in time. Strong painkillers like codeine don’t help and can cause their own problems.
model.why: Plain explanation, including why painkillers fail

model.text: So that’s why nothing’s worked.

For the attacks there are two treatments that work. One is an injection you give yourself under the skin, called sumatriptan, or a nasal spray version. Before that, a couple of questions — any heart problems, chest pain, or high blood pressure you know of?
model.why: Offers subcutaneous or nasal triptan and checks cautions

model.text: Not that I know of.

I’ll check your blood pressure before you go. The other treatment is oxygen through a special mask at a high flow, started as soon as an attack begins — many people find it switches the attack off in minutes. I can arrange oxygen at home and a portable cylinder.
model.why: High-flow oxygen with home and ambulatory supply (NICE CG150)

model.text: Oxygen? I smoke, is that a problem?

It’s an important question. Oxygen makes things burn fiercely, so you must never smoke, vape or have a flame near it. The oxygen company will do a safety check at home. This could also be a good moment to think about stopping smoking — would you like support with that?
model.why: Addresses the fire risk and offers smoking support

model.text: I’ll think about it. Honestly, if it stops these, I’d try.

To stop the attacks coming, there’s a preventive tablet called verapamil. It can slow the heart’s electrical system, so it needs heart tracings as the dose goes up. I’ll get specialist advice on starting it and refer you to the headache team, who will also decide whether you need a scan, as this is your first bout.
model.why: Prevention with specialist advice and ECG monitoring; neuroimaging discussion for a first bout

model.text: Is there anything I should avoid?
While you’re in a bout, alcohol often triggers an attack, so avoid it until the bout is over. How are you managing with work and sleep?
model.why: Trigger advice and checks practical impact

model.text: Barely. I’m wrecked in the day.
If you need time off while we get this under control, I can give you a fit note. Does this plan feel right to you?
model.why: Offers practical support and checks agreement

model.text: Yes. It’s the first time I’ve felt anyone knows what this is.

A sudden thunderclap headache, weakness, numbness, speech or vision problems, or fever with a stiff neck — that’s 999 or A&E, because that isn’t cluster headache. If your mood drops or you feel unsafe, contact us the same day or NHS 111. Can you tell me back what the plan is?
model.why: Specific red-flag and mood safety net, then teach-back

model.text: Injection or spray at the start of an attack, oxygen at home with no smoking near it, verapamil once the specialist advises, no drink during the bout, 999 for a sudden or different headache.
That’s exactly it. I’ll see you again in a week to see how the treatment is working and to check the heart tracing plan.

social.t: Nightly attacks wreck sleep and daytime function. Ask about work demands and offer a fit note while the bout is brought under control.
Smoking is linked with cluster headache and is a fire risk with home oxygen. Offer referral to local stop-smoking support; very brief advice is enough to start.

legal.t: Home and ambulatory oxygen is ordered through the local home oxygen order process, with a home safety risk assessment; the patient signs consent to the supplier’s safety conditions.
A fit note can be issued if he is unfit for work while the bout is controlled; it can advise adjusted hours if nights are disrupted.

professional.t: NICE CG150 advises seeking specialist advice before starting verapamil if unfamiliar with its use in cluster headache — working within competence (GMC Good medical practice).
Ask directly; do not rely on risk scales (NICE NG225). Record thoughts, protective factors and the agreed safety plan.

community.t: OUCH (UK) cluster headache charity and the Migraine Trust for patient information and peer support; NHS stop-smoking services.

redFlags: Thunderclap or first-and-worst headache — same-day emergency assessment
Focal neurology, visual loss, fever with neck stiffness, a changing pattern or raised-pressure features
ice: Concern: a tumour; the unbearable pain
Expectation: for someone to stop the pain

playbook.diagnosis: First bout of episodic cluster headache (a trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia): strictly right-sided orbital pain for about an hour, nightly at 2am for two weeks, with ipsilateral tearing, red eye and rhinorrhoea, restlessness, and a normal examination.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “It’s called cluster headache. It comes in bouts, often at the same time each day, and it’s one of the most painful conditions there is. It isn’t a tumour and it isn’t migraine — and it has its own treatments that work.”

management.reflectIce: “You wondered about migraine, sinuses and even a tumour. What you describe is a well-recognised pattern, and your examination is normal.”
management.psychosocial: Ask about suicidal thoughts and agree a safety plan; fit note if needed; smoking support linked to oxygen safety.
sharedPlan: Subcutaneous or nasal triptan with enough supply for attack frequency, after checking cautions (NICE CG150; BNF)
100% oxygen at 12 L/min or more via non-rebreathing mask with reservoir bag; home and ambulatory supply (NICE CG150)
No paracetamol, NSAIDs, opioids, ergots or oral triptans for attacks (NICE CG150)
Verapamil for prevention with specialist advice and ECG monitoring; referral to the headache or neurology service, including whether imaging is needed for a first bout
Avoid alcohol during the bout; no smoking near oxygen; stop-smoking support
safetyNet: 999 or A&E for thunderclap headache, new neurological symptoms, or fever with neck stiffness
Same-day contact, NHS 111 or 999 if suicidal thoughts increase or he feels unsafe

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by treating cluster headache as a bad migraine. The history gives the diagnosis away; the marks are in the specific acute plan, safety and the man in front of you.

items.why: Short, strictly one-sided attacks with autonomic signs and restlessness are cluster headache.
items.fix: Ask about restlessness versus lying still, side, duration and timing, then name it.

items.why: NICE CG150 says do not offer opioids, paracetamol, NSAIDs, ergots or oral triptans for acute cluster attacks.
items.fix: Subcutaneous or nasal triptan and/or high-flow oxygen.

items.fail: Ordering oxygen without discussing his smoking.
items.why: Home oxygen near cigarettes is a fire risk.
items.fix: Explain the rule clearly and offer stop-smoking support.

items.fail: Starting verapamil with no plan for ECG monitoring.
items.why: Verapamil can cause heart block as the dose rises.
items.fix: Seek specialist advice and plan ECGs, as NICE CG150 advises.

items.why: Hopelessness during a bout is common and the pain is extreme.
items.fix: Ask directly and kindly; agree a safety plan.

items.why: He needs to know which headaches are different and dangerous.
items.fix: Name the red flags, say 999, and book a review in a week.

Eyes and neurology; name cluster headache and why painkillers fail.

999 for sudden or different headache; mood safety net; review in a week; teach-back.

wordPics.exc: All of that, plus: explains clearly why tablets fail; asks directly and kindly about suicidal thoughts and agrees a safety plan; addresses smoking and oxygen safety without judgement; plans verapamil with specialist advice and ECG monitoring; gives a fit note; teach-back; he leaves with hope.

avoid.dont: “It sounds like a migraine — try sumatriptan tablets.”
avoid.instead: “This is cluster headache. Tablets are too slow, so we use an injection or nasal spray, and oxygen.”
avoid.why: NICE CG150 advises against oral triptans for acute cluster attacks.

avoid.dont: “I’ll give you something stronger, like co-codamol.”
avoid.instead: “Strong painkillers don’t help these attacks — let’s use treatments that do.”
avoid.why: Opioids are ineffective here and carry harm; NICE CG150 says do not offer them.

I’d like to examine your eyes, face and nervous system. … Your pupils, eye movements and the back of your eyes look normal, and the nerve checks are normal. Together with your story, this fits cluster headache, not migraine and not a tumour or sinuses.
SCA_MODELS.why: Examines and names the diagnosis with the reasoning

SCA_MODELS.text: Cluster headache? I’ve never heard of it.

It’s a headache that comes in bouts — often weeks at a time — usually at the same time each day. The pain is one-sided around the eye, with the eye watering and the nose running on that side, and people can’t keep still. Tablets fail because each attack is too short and too fierce for a tablet to be absorbed in time. Strong painkillers like codeine don’t help and can cause their own problems.
SCA_MODELS.why: Plain explanation, including why painkillers fail

SCA_MODELS.text: So that’s why nothing’s worked.

For the attacks there are two treatments that work. One is an injection you give yourself under the skin, called sumatriptan, or a nasal spray version. Before that, a couple of questions — any heart problems, chest pain, or high blood pressure you know of?
SCA_MODELS.why: Offers subcutaneous or nasal triptan and checks cautions

SCA_MODELS.text: Not that I know of.

I’ll check your blood pressure before you go. The other treatment is oxygen through a special mask at a high flow, started as soon as an attack begins — many people find it switches the attack off in minutes. I can arrange oxygen at home and a portable cylinder.
SCA_MODELS.why: High-flow oxygen with home and ambulatory supply (NICE CG150)

SCA_MODELS.text: Oxygen? I smoke, is that a problem?

It’s an important question. Oxygen makes things burn fiercely, so you must never smoke, vape or have a flame near it. The oxygen company will do a safety check at home. This could also be a good moment to think about stopping smoking — would you like support with that?
SCA_MODELS.why: Addresses the fire risk and offers smoking support

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ll think about it. Honestly, if it stops these, I’d try.

To stop the attacks coming, there’s a preventive tablet called verapamil. It can slow the heart’s electrical system, so it needs heart tracings as the dose goes up. I’ll get specialist advice on starting it and refer you to the headache team, who will also decide whether you need a scan, as this is your first bout.
SCA_MODELS.why: Prevention with specialist advice and ECG monitoring; neuroimaging discussion for a first bout

SCA_MODELS.text: Is there anything I should avoid?
While you’re in a bout, alcohol often triggers an attack, so avoid it until the bout is over. How are you managing with work and sleep?
SCA_MODELS.why: Trigger advice and checks practical impact

SCA_MODELS.text: Barely. I’m wrecked in the day.
If you need time off while we get this under control, I can give you a fit note. Does this plan feel right to you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Offers practical support and checks agreement

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes. It’s the first time I’ve felt anyone knows what this is.

A sudden thunderclap headache, weakness, numbness, speech or vision problems, or fever with a stiff neck — that’s 999 or A&E, because that isn’t cluster headache. If your mood drops or you feel unsafe, contact us the same day or NHS 111. Can you tell me back what the plan is?
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific red-flag and mood safety net, then teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: Injection or spray at the start of an attack, oxygen at home with no smoking near it, verapamil once the specialist advises, no drink during the bout, 999 for a sudden or different headache.
That’s exactly it. I’ll see you again in a week to see how the treatment is working and to check the heart tracing plan.

SCA_STEM.name: Marek Solomon
meds: Over-the-counter painkillers for the headaches — no benefit
SCA_STEM.recent: Two weeks of nightly attacks of severe right-sided pain behind the eye, around 2am, lasting about an hour, with a red watering eye and a runny right nostril. No previous consultation about them.
SCA_STEM.reason: “These headaches are destroying me — painkillers do nothing.”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE CG150 (headaches in over 12s: diagnosis and management, 2012, updated June 2025) · [2] NICE NG225 (self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence, 2022) · [3] International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (International Headache Society, 2018) (international)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Strictly one-sided, severe pain around the eye lasting about an hour, at the same time each night for two weeks, with a red watering eye, a runny nostril on the same side and pacing restlessness, is cluster headache. Name it, explain why tablets fail, and give the acute plan NICE CG150 sets out: high-flow oxygen and/or a subcutaneous or nasal triptan. Consider verapamil for prevention with specialist advice and ECG monitoring, screen red flags and mood, and deal with the smoking and home-oxygen safety issue.

points.t: Attacks of severe unilateral orbital, supraorbital or temporal pain lasting roughly 15–180 minutes, from every other day up to several a day, with ipsilateral autonomic features (tearing, red eye, nasal blockage or discharge, lid swelling or drooping, small pupil) and/or restlessness or agitation [3]. Bouts often last weeks and recur at the same time of day. It is commoner in men and in smokers.

Migraine usually lasts hours to days, is often throbbing with nausea and light sensitivity, and the person lies still in a dark room. In cluster headache the person cannot keep still, the attacks are short and strictly one-sided, and the autonomic signs are on the painful side. Sinusitis does not wake someone at the same hour every night with a streaming eye.

NICE CG150 [1]: offer oxygen and/or a subcutaneous or nasal triptan. Oxygen is 100% at a flow rate of at least 12 litres per minute through a non-rebreathing mask with a reservoir bag, with home and ambulatory oxygen arranged. Make sure the triptan supply is enough for the attack frequency. Do not offer paracetamol, NSAIDs, opioids, ergots or oral triptans for acute attacks [1]. Check triptan cautions such as ischaemic heart disease and uncontrolled hypertension (BNF).

NICE CG150 [1]: consider verapamil for prevention during a bout; if unfamiliar with its use for cluster headache, seek specialist advice first, including advice on ECG monitoring, because heart block can develop as the dose rises (BNF). Seek specialist advice if verapamil does not work. Steroid courses and occipital nerve blocks are specialist options to break a bout.

NICE CG150 [1]: discuss the need for neuroimaging for a first bout of cluster headache with a GP with a special interest in headache or a neurologist. Red flags needing urgent assessment include thunderclap onset, new neurological deficit, fever with neck stiffness, a changing pattern, features of raised pressure, and new headache in older age.

Home oxygen is ordered through the home oxygen order process with a safety risk assessment. Smoking, vaping or naked flames near oxygen are a serious fire risk, so an honest conversation about smoking is a safety step as well as a health one.

The pain is among the most severe known and hopelessness during a bout is common. Ask directly about suicidal thoughts; NICE NG225 [2] advises against using risk scales to predict outcome — assess needs and agree a safety plan.
Alcohol commonly triggers attacks during a bout but not between bouts, so advise avoiding it while a bout is active. Support to stop smoking.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let him describe the pain, timing, eye and nose symptoms and the pacing before narrowing.
Asked about sleep, work, smoking and alcohol, and how the bout was affecting daily life.
Picked up ‘destroying me’, head-banging and 3am fears; asked directly about suicidal thoughts.
Idea: migraine or sinuses. Concern: a tumour and the unbearable pain. Expectation: for the pain to stop.
Examined pupils, lids, fundi and neurology; checked BP before triptan; noted ECG monitoring for verapamil.
Cluster headache versus migraine, sinusitis, trigeminal neuralgia and secondary headache.
Screened thunderclap onset, focal neurology, visual change, fever and neck stiffness; screened suicidality.
Cluster headache (first bout) explained clearly, including why tablets fail.
Subcutaneous or nasal triptan and high-flow 100% oxygen at 12 L/min or more (NICE CG150); no opioids or oral analgesics; verapamil with specialist advice.
Smoking and oxygen fire risk with cessation support; alcohol during a bout; fit note; neuroimaging discussion for a first bout.
999 for red-flag headache, same-day contact for worsening mood; review in a week; teach-back.

social.t: Nightly attacks wreck sleep and daytime function. Ask about work demands and offer a fit note while the bout is brought under control.
Smoking is linked with cluster headache and is a fire risk with home oxygen. Offer referral to local stop-smoking support; very brief advice is enough to start.

legal.t: Home and ambulatory oxygen is ordered through the local home oxygen order process, with a home safety risk assessment; the patient signs consent to the supplier’s safety conditions.
A fit note can be issued if he is unfit for work while the bout is controlled; it can advise adjusted hours if nights are disrupted.

professional.t: NICE CG150 advises seeking specialist advice before starting verapamil if unfamiliar with its use in cluster headache — working within competence (GMC Good medical practice).
Ask directly; do not rely on risk scales (NICE NG225). Record thoughts, protective factors and the agreed safety plan.

community.t: OUCH (UK) cluster headache charity and the Migraine Trust for patient information and peer support; NHS stop-smoking services.

redFlags: Thunderclap or first-and-worst headache — same-day emergency assessment
Focal neurology, visual loss, fever with neck stiffness, a changing pattern or raised-pressure features
ice: Concern: a tumour; the unbearable pain
Expectation: for someone to stop the pain

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: First bout of episodic cluster headache (a trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia): strictly right-sided orbital pain for about an hour, nightly at 2am for two weeks, with ipsilateral tearing, red eye and rhinorrhoea, restlessness, and a normal examination.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “It’s called cluster headache. It comes in bouts, often at the same time each day, and it’s one of the most painful conditions there is. It isn’t a tumour and it isn’t migraine — and it has its own treatments that work.”

management.reflectIce: “You wondered about migraine, sinuses and even a tumour. What you describe is a well-recognised pattern, and your examination is normal.”
management.psychosocial: Ask about suicidal thoughts and agree a safety plan; fit note if needed; smoking support linked to oxygen safety.
sharedPlan: Subcutaneous or nasal triptan with enough supply for attack frequency, after checking cautions (NICE CG150; BNF)
100% oxygen at 12 L/min or more via non-rebreathing mask with reservoir bag; home and ambulatory supply (NICE CG150)
No paracetamol, NSAIDs, opioids, ergots or oral triptans for attacks (NICE CG150)
Verapamil for prevention with specialist advice and ECG monitoring; referral to the headache or neurology service, including whether imaging is needed for a first bout
Avoid alcohol during the bout; no smoking near oxygen; stop-smoking support
safetyNet: 999 or A&E for thunderclap headache, new neurological symptoms, or fever with neck stiffness
Same-day contact, NHS 111 or 999 if suicidal thoughts increase or he feels unsafe

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by treating cluster headache as a bad migraine. The history gives the diagnosis away; the marks are in the specific acute plan, safety and the man in front of you.

items.why: Short, strictly one-sided attacks with autonomic signs and restlessness are cluster headache.
items.fix: Ask about restlessness versus lying still, side, duration and timing, then name it.

items.why: NICE CG150 says do not offer opioids, paracetamol, NSAIDs, ergots or oral triptans for acute cluster attacks.
items.fix: Subcutaneous or nasal triptan and/or high-flow oxygen.

items.fail: Ordering oxygen without discussing his smoking.
items.why: Home oxygen near cigarettes is a fire risk.
items.fix: Explain the rule clearly and offer stop-smoking support.

items.fail: Starting verapamil with no plan for ECG monitoring.
items.why: Verapamil can cause heart block as the dose rises.
items.fix: Seek specialist advice and plan ECGs, as NICE CG150 advises.

items.why: Hopelessness during a bout is common and the pain is extreme.
items.fix: Ask directly and kindly; agree a safety plan.

items.why: He needs to know which headaches are different and dangerous.
items.fix: Name the red flags, say 999, and book a review in a week.
